claims.text: Al-containing CrFeCoNiAl forms a continuous, coherent, slow-growing Al2O3 scale above 900 °C.
The Al2O3 scale persists and protects the underlying alloy from further oxidation or corrosion.
CrFeCoNi alloys lacking Al form discontinuous, unstable oxide scales that crack or spall.
Both the CrFeCoNiAl alloy and its CrFeCoNi or low-Al baseline can be prepared as single-phase solid solutions with matched processing and impurity levels.
Al content is the only intended varying parameter between the test alloy and baseline.
A continuous Al2O3 layer at the metal/oxide interface acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
A coherent interfacial Al2O3 layer minimizes internal stress or stress accumulation.
Al preferentially oxidizes because of its high oxygen affinity.
Al2O3 grows slowly because it has low oxygen diffusivity.
Reduced oxygen ingress lowers the rate of subsequent alloy oxidation.
A low-Al or Al-free baseline lacks sufficient Al to establish the proposed protective Al2O3 layer.
Nonuniform and discontinuous oxides on the baseline crack and spall under thermal and mechanical stresses.
Under identical exposure conditions, CrFeCoNiAl will have a lower oxide growth rate than the baseline.
CrFeCoNiAl will have a more coherent and adherent scale with less spallation than the baseline.
The baseline will exhibit cracked scales and a higher effective oxidation rate.
The proposed behavior applies above 900 °C in oxidizing or mildly corrosive environments for single-phase solid-solution alloys.
The proposed behavior may not extrapolate to multiphase alloys or environments containing extreme corrosive species.
Similar scale growth and cracking or spallation in the Al-containing alloy and baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The comparison is not uniquely defined: the baseline is alternately specified as Al-free CrFeCoNi or an unspecified low-Al alloy. Those controls test different contrasts and leave the operative Al threshold undefined.

If the formulas CrFeCoNi and CrFeCoNiAl denote equiatomic alloys, their Cr, Fe, Co, and Ni atomic percentages are 25% and 20%, respectively, so they are not compositionally identical apart from Al in atomic-percentage terms.
